The Week Immigration Enforcement Became a Speech Test

Detentions of pro-Palestinian students, a defiant DOJ directive to ignore courts, and the start of dismantling the Education Department marked a week of escalating executive reach

```markdown The week of March 8 to 14 opened with an arrest that would echo through nearly every day that followed. Immigration agents detained Mahmoud Khalil, a legal permanent resident and recent Columbia graduate, and moved him to a detention facility in Louisiana without filing criminal charges. The administration invoked a rarely used provision allowing deportation over alleged foreign-policy risk, and President Trump said the arrest was only the first in a campaign against pro-Palestinian activists. That declaration proved accurate: over the following days, the case against Khalil widened into a broader pattern of using immigration law as a tool against political speech—one of the week's defining threads.

The weekend also brought other signs of institutional friction. The Supreme Court rejected an attempt by the administration to freeze nearly $2 billion in foreign aid that Congress had already approved, reaffirming that spending power does not belong to the executive alone. At the same time, the Justice Department dropped a long-running environmental-justice case tied to Louisiana's "Cancer Alley," and Trump dismissed the chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff along with other senior military leaders—a move sudden enough that five former defense secretaries called for immediate congressional hearings over fears the armed forces were being reshaped along political lines. Meanwhile, the DOJ removed senior national-security officials in favor of ideological allies, and DHS began polygraphing its own employees to hunt for leaks about ICE operations. Outside government, the pushback was already visible in the streets: protests against Elon Musk's role in the administration spread to Tesla dealerships nationwide, more than 150 "Stand Up for Science" events took place, and Bernie Sanders' "Fighting Oligarchy" tour drew large crowds.

By Monday, courts had begun to answer back. U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman ordered that Khalil not be deported while his case proceeded, offering the first judicial check on the new campaign against activist students—though it did nothing to slow the broader effort. That same day, Attorney General Pam Bondi dismantled Task Force KleptoCapture, paused enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act for six months, and disbanded the FBI's foreign-influence taskforce, stripping away institutional capacity built to track oligarch wealth and foreign interference. Elsewhere, a federal judge ordered Musk's DOGE office to comply with transparency law and release internal records, and a separate ruling found that a presidential pardon for a January 6 defendant did not extend to an unrelated plot to kill federal agents. Trump also endorsed a stopgap funding bill that would boost defense spending while cutting non-defense programs, setting up a fight that would carry into the following days.

Tuesday sharpened two threads that would define the rest of the week. The Department of Education fired more than 1,300 employees in a single day, cutting its workforce roughly in half and eliminating more than half of its Civil Rights Division offices—a preview of a formal dismantling order still to come. Separately, a presidential memorandum instructed federal agencies to ask courts to impose financial bonds on parties seeking injunctions against government action, calling recent court rulings against the administration "meritless." A federal judge in Boston blocked planned cuts to teacher-training funding, and new FBI director Kash Patel relocated as many as 1,500 agents amid concern the bureau's focus would shift toward left-leaning protest groups rather than far-right extremism. The day's most serious lapse, however, involved national security directly: National Security Adviser Mike Waltz accidentally added a journalist to a Signal group chat where officials were discussing classified strike planning in Yemen. Trump later dismissed the breach as a minor "glitch," even as the Senate Armed Services Committee demanded a Pentagon inspector general investigation.

Wednesday brought the week's clearest run of judicial resistance. Federal Judge Beryl Howell ruled that Trump's executive order stripping security clearances and contracts from the law firm Perkins Coie violated the First Amendment, comparing it to an unconstitutional bill of attainder—an early sign of a pattern that would recur before the week was out. Judge William Alsup found the government's stated justifications for mass federal layoffs to be false and ordered reinstatement of workers across multiple agencies, while another court compelled DOGE to produce records on its cost-cutting operations. Those operations came under further strain when an independent tracker found that Musk's claimed $105 billion in government savings was verifiable only to about $8.6 billion—a gap Musk criticized without addressing. Trade policy also escalated that day: 25 percent tariffs on imported steel and aluminum took effect, prompting the European Union to announce roughly $28 billion in retaliatory tariffs and Canada about $21 billion. And in a case with implications beyond any single individual, Judge Paula Xinis found that the government had acted with no legal basis in detaining and deporting Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant with legal work authorization, despite a prior court order—calling the government's conduct "wholly lawless."

Thursday deepened both the education and immigration threads. More than twenty Democratic attorneys general, led by New York's Letitia James, sued to block the Education Department layoffs, arguing the cuts were unconstitutional and would harm students with disabilities and low-income households—setting up a direct legal test of whether the executive branch could unilaterally gut a cabinet agency. On the immigration front, attorneys alleged that ICE had obtained a search warrant on false pretenses, framed as an investigation into Columbia "harboring aliens" but aimed instead at pro-Palestinian activist students Yunseo Chung and Ranjani Srinivasan; agents searched dorm rooms, and Srinivasan left the country after her visa was revoked. Their cases were distinct from Khalil's, but part of the same expanding campaign. Far more severe in scale, federal agents secretly flew at least 252 Venezuelan migrants to a "terrorism confinement" prison in El Salvador based on gang-affiliation allegations, without a public registry of names or charges; many families learned of the transfers only through news reports weeks later. Separately, nearly 100 protesters were arrested at Trump Tower after occupying its lobby to demand Khalil's release, and in the Senate, ten Democrats joined Republicans to advance the House funding bill via cloture, prompting sharp criticism within their own party over how much spending discretion the deal ceded to the administration.

Friday consolidated nearly every strand of the week into a single, dense set of executive actions. Trump signed an order directing Education Secretary Linda McMahon to begin dismantling the department outright, formalizing what the layoffs had already begun—though full elimination would still require Congress. Days after a court struck down the punitive order against Perkins Coie, Trump signed a nearly identical order against Paul Weiss, suspending security clearances, terminating government contracts, and restricting building access over the firm's past representation of January 6 defendants—confirming that the targeting of law firms was a pattern rather than an isolated case. Trump also invoked the Alien Enemies Act, an 1798 wartime statute, to declare members of the Tren de Aragua gang subject to summary apprehension and removal without standard immigration due process—an extraordinary use of law rarely invoked outside declared wars, extending the logic of Thursday's covert deportations into formal policy. That expansion of unilateral authority was matched by an explicit challenge to the courts themselves: a senior DOJ official told immigration lawyers that deportation flights "need to take off, no matter what," and that if a court tried to stop them, the department might tell the court "f— you." At a Justice Department event the same day, Trump denounced former special counsel Jack Smith and other investigators as "bad people" who had tried to turn America into a "third-world country," while separately celebrating the dismissal of a corruption case against New York's mayor. A further executive order moved to eliminate or shrink seven federal entities, including the U.S. Agency for Global Media, defunding Voice of America and Radio Free Asia and putting contracted journalists in authoritarian countries at heightened personal risk. Even amid this surge, the judiciary did not go silent: Judge James Bredar issued a temporary restraining order blocking further firings at eighteen federal agencies, finding the government likely engaged in an illegal scheme, adding to Wednesday's reinstatement ruling.

Taken as a whole, the week showed two forces moving in direct tension. Federal courts intervened repeatedly and specifically—blocking a deportation, reinstating fired workers, striking down a law firm sanction, halting further firings—demonstrating that institutional checks were still functioning and willing to rule against the executive branch on the merits. But the week's final days revealed something new: an official readiness, voiced plainly by a senior Justice Department lawyer, to disregard a court order altogether if it stood in the way of deportation flights. Paired with the invocation of a wartime statute to bypass ordinary due process, the dismantling of a cabinet department by executive order, and a second law firm punished despite a court's rebuke of the first, the week marked less a single crisis than an accumulation—each action testing how far unilateral power could reach before the courts, Congress, or the public pushed back, and whether that pushback would still be enough. ```
